bib.title: PLAY2PROMPT: Zero-shot Tool Instruction Optimization for LLM Agents via Tool Play

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Play2Prompt: Zero-shot Tool Instruction Optimization for LLM Agents via Tool Play", Wei Fang, Yang Zhang, Kaizhi Qian, James Glass, Yada Zhu (MIT; MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab). arXiv 2503.14432v2, 12 Jun 2025. The extraction names no venue, so treat it as a preprint. The layout looks ACL-style, but I can't confirm that.

COVERAGE: 66209 of 66209 chars read. That covers the main text, limitations, Tables 1-17, Appendices A-F and the meta-prompts. The references were only skimmed. The figures' internal content (Fig 3 and Fig 4 trajectories) is not in the text extraction. I read only the captions and the surrounding prose.

FIT WARNING: Fit is good for "improve tool docs and demos by playing with the tool, zero-shot". It is not about planning. It covers only single-tool description and example optimization, evaluated on tool-calling accuracy. Say so in the chapter, and place it under tool use rather than planning.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Playing with each tool, then rewriting its docs and generating demos, raises BFCL Executable accuracy for all six task models.
  - number: Avg accuracy, baseline to +P2P: LLaMA-8B 85.9 to 92.9; LLaMA-70B 90.8 to 94.5; GPT-3.5 87.0 to 92.5; GPT-4o 92.4 to 94.9; ToolACE-8B 87.4 to 90.3; Hammer-7B 82.6 to 87.2.
  - setup: BFCL Executable, 310 queries, 5 categories. Zero-shot baseline with official prompts or function-calling mode. Optimizer is llama-3.1-8b-instruct. 5 demos per tool at inference. Scores averaged over 3 runs. No variance is reported.
  - quote: "absolute gains of 4-7% are observed for the open models and GPT-3.5, while GPT-4o achieves 3% in-crease in average accuracy despite its already high baseline."
  - where: Sec 3.2, Table 1 (pp. 5-6).
- It also helps on StableToolBench, a harder multi-tool benchmark run with ReAct, and beats EasyTool and DRAFT where those were run.
  - number: Avg solvable pass rate, ReAct to +P2P: LLaMA-8B 55.8 to 62.2; LLaMA-70B 63.1 to 69.2; GPT-3.5 60.7 to 65.9; GPT-4o 62.8 to 64.9. EasyTool gives 56.7, 65.6, 63.1 and 60.5 for the same four models.
  - setup: 790 queries over six subsets and 2479 APIs. Judge is llama-3.3-70b-instruct. 1 demo per tool. EasyTool uses the authors' released docs under StableToolBench ReAct prompts. DRAFT was run only on I2-Cat and I3-Inst, using its released docs.
  - quote: "PLAY2PROMPT also consistent across subsets" and "EasyTool degrades GPT-4o on all subsets, whereas PLAY2PROMPT achieves a 2% improvement on average."
  - where: Table 2 and its text (p. 6). The text says "5-7%" for the LLaMA models and GPT-3.5.
- The gain grows as documentation gets worse.
  - number: Parameter-description dropout p=0, 0.5, 1.0. Mean weighted gain is 5.0% at p=0.0 and 7.1% at p=1.0. At p=0.5, GPT-3.5 goes 77.8 to 87.3 Avg, against 87.0 undegraded. At p=1.0, GPT-4o goes 79.2 to 85.0 Avg.
  - setup: BFCL Executable. Parameter descriptions are dropped at random. The tool description and parameter names are kept.
  - quote: "average improvements growing from 5.0% at p = 0.0 and reaching 7.1% at p = 1.0."
  - where: Fig 2, Tables 8-9, App C.
- Demonstrations matter more than rewritten docs in most cases, and the two together are best.
  - number: LLaMA-8B BFCL: Desc 89.9, Demo 90.8, both 92.9. LLaMA-70B BFCL: Desc 93.6, Demo 92.7, both 94.5. GPT-3.5 BFCL: Desc 89.0, Demo 91.9, both 92.5. STB, LLaMA-70B: Desc 64.4, Demo 67.8, both 69.2.
  - setup: Ablation, Table 3.
  - quote: "employing only optimized demonstrations yields larger improvements than solely relying on optimized documentation, and combining both consistently achieves the best results."
  - where: Table 3 (p. 7).
  - Caveat: the text overstates the case. In Table 3, LLaMA-70B on BFCL has docs-only (93.6) above demos-only (92.7).
- Rewarding examples the task model fails on beats rewarding only example quality.
  - number: STB avg, LLaMA-8B: 60.7 (Easy) vs 62.2. LLaMA-70B: 68.2 vs 69.2.
  - setup: Removes the R_e term (the difficulty reward), keeping only R_q (the example-quality reward).
  - quote: "Ignoring difficult examples reduces final performance by an average of 1-2% across all subsets"
  - where: Table 4 (p. 7-8). The supporting figure shows 1.0 to 1.5 points on average.
- Search depth and reflection steps buy accuracy at proportional cost.
  - number: I3-Inst, LLaMA-70B pass rate: ReAct 64.3; MC depth 1 gives 65.2 (3 proposals); MC depth 5 gives 66.7 (15); MC depth 5 with NE=3 gives 68.9 (45); Beam depth 5 with NE=3 gives 70.7 (135).
  - quote: "Beam search (depth = 5) & NE= 3 70.7 135"
  - where: Table 5.
  - Note: the main runs use depth 3, L=3 and W=10 on BFCL and W=3 on STB. Table 5 is a different configuration.
- Generated examples and docs are rated about as good as human-curated ones.
  - number: Naturalness 4.17 vs 4.39, alignment 4.52 vs 4.68 (1-5 scale). Completeness win rate vs raw docs: 85% on STB, 79% on BFCL. Conciseness: P2P wins only 35% on STB and 15% on BFCL, while raw wins 47% and 70%.
  - setup: 6 annotators, 50 doc outputs and 30 examples.
  - quote: "our optimized documentation achieves significantly higher completeness and comparable or better accuracy, though with reduced conciseness due to increased verbosity."
  - where: Tables 6-7 (p. 9).
- Method mechanics worth teaching:
  - Examples are built in reverse. Explore valid invocations first, observe the output, then write the query and answer.
  - Reward for examples: R = R_q + λR_e, with λ=1. R_e is the negative of the task model's score with the original docs and no demos, so it favours hard examples.
  - Reward for docs: the task model's score on the generated examples used as a validation set. The two objectives are adversarial.
  - quote: "we generate samples in reverse order: first, we explore valid invocations Ik, ob-serve the tool's output, and then construct a corresponding query x and answer y."
  - where: Sec 2.4-2.5.

BASELINES
- BFCL: the baseline is zero-shot with no docs or examples added.
  - There is no baseline of hand-written docs or demos.
  - There is no baseline of the same compute spent on few-shot sampling.
  - There is no comparison against simply giving the model a better prompt.
- StableToolBench: EasyTool and DRAFT are run, but not matched.
  - EasyTool needs labeled docs and examples from other tools, so it is not zero-shot. It also uses different inference prompts.
  - DRAFT results exist only for two subsets, using its released docs. DRAFT's optimizer was GPT-4o, versus llama-3.1-8b here.
- Cost of the exploration phase: not reported per tool.
  - Appendix B says "An estimated 1M API calls were made in total for this work" and that GPU hours are not reported.
  - Table 5 is the only cost view: 3 to 135 proposals explored per run. Per-tool cost for the main configuration is not given.
- Statistics: scores are averaged over 3 runs, with no confidence intervals. BFCL categories are small (50 queries in Multiple, 40 in Multiple-Parallel). That size is inferred from the percentage steps, not stated.

LIMITS
- The authors concede that optimization is single-tool only. Multi-tool queries work by optimizing each tool independently and concatenating the results.
- Rejection sampling fails for functions with huge parameter spaces, such as long ID strings or auth tokens that need other tool calls first.
- Only docs and demos are optimized. Other information is left as "meta-information".
- Not shown by the paper:
  - Executable tools are required (BFCL Executable, cached or simulated RapidAPI). Side-effecting tools (writes, deletes, payments) are not addressed.
  - Nothing is said about doc length or token cost at inference, even though the docs are acknowledged to be more verbose.
  - There is no comparison with larger optimizer models.
  - Gains are not uniform. BFCL Simple-REST for GPT-4o falls 98.6 to 95.7. ToolACE and Hammer fall on Simple-Python (96.0 to 95.0 and 96.0 to 95.0). GPT-4o on STB falls on I1-Cat, I2-Inst and I2-Cat (69.7 to 68.7, 59.8 to 58.8, 65.3 to 63.7).
  - The judge on StableToolBench is a LLaMA model, not a human.
- Dated: BFCL and StableToolBench versions from 2024-2025 and GPT-3.5/GPT-4o-class models. Modern frontier models and MCP-style tool descriptions are untested.

BUILDS ON
- Beam-search prompt optimization: Wang et al. 2024 (PromptAgent) and Pryzant et al. 2023 (ProTeGi).
- Self-reflection: Madaan et al. 2023 (Self-Refine), Shinn et al. 2023 (Reflexion).
- Tool documentation: Hsieh et al. 2023 (Tool documentation enables zero-shot tool usage).
- ReAct: Yao et al. 2023.
- Hard-example selection: Yoo and Kweon 2019 (active learning).
- Competing methods: Yuan et al. 2024 (EasyTool), Qu et al. 2025 (DRAFT), Shen et al. 2024 (TaskBench).
- Benchmarks: Yan et al. 2024 (BFCL), Guo et al. 2024 (StableToolBench), Qin et al. 2024b (ToolLLM).

CODE (prompts worth keeping, App F)
- m1, page 15, invocation proposer. Key line: "The generated API call must be executable and real. Parameter values must be filled in and not placeholding text." Its output format is `{"name": "function_name","parameters": {"properties": {"parameter_1": value 1}}}`, and it carries a log of previous calls with outputs and reflections.
- m2, page 15, error critic. Its key rule: "Note that even if the "error" field in the result is empty, the "response" field may contain an error when using the function call." It returns `{"analysis":..., "err_code": -1|0}`.
- m3, page 16, query generation. Rule: "You must not include specific function calls in your response. You should also never explicitly name the parameter names". The query must contain every parameter value.
- m5, page 16, quality scorer, 1-3. It scores 1 for leaked function or parameter names, queries over 3 sentences or 300 letters, or any parameter value missing from the query.
- m7 and m8, page 17, doc rewriter and doc critic. The rewriter is told to maximize the score and minimize the stdev, and to describe every required and optional parameter with its type, usage and possible values. The critic must "Identify how the descriptions affect the function call errors" and contrast good descriptions (score above 60%) with bad ones.
- Pseudocode: Algorithms 1-2 on page 14. Algorithm 1 is the loop of sample invocation, execute, LLM-verify, then query, answer, score, reflect.

FIGURE: Figure 1, page 3, the framework diagram. It shows the two beam-search stages: tool-play to examples, then examples as a validation set to docs. It also shows that documentation and demos both feed the task LLM at inference. Figure 3 (p. 8) is a good runner-up. It is a qualitative trajectory where the doc claims `start_date` and `end_date` but the real parameters are `from` and `to`, and the search converges to the right names by reading error feedback.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found in the text.
- The extraction is clean. Tables are flattened, and the Table 1 columns are readable in order: Simple-Python, Simple-REST, Multiple, Parallel, Multiple-Parallel, Weighted Avg, Avg. Figure internals (Fig 2 bars, Fig 3, Fig 4) are not extracted. Fig 2's labels came out only as a list of percentages that I could not map to models.
- The paper's text and tables disagree in places. The text says "4-7%" for gains and the tables fit that. The "demos beat docs" claim fails for LLaMA-70B on BFCL (Table 3). I did not verify the paper's own arithmetic beyond that.
- The "Easy" ablation (Table 4) and "5-7%" gains use averages with no variance, so small differences are weak evidence.
